title: The Honest Shepherd and the Sharper

full_text:
An affluent landowner in Egypt entrusted a flock of five hundred sheep to an honest young shepherd named Mansur. The landowner praised the shepherd’s integrity so highly at the coffee-houses of Cairo that a cynical sharper wagered fifty gold dinars that he could induce the shepherd to sell him a lamb without his master's knowledge.

The sharper traveled to the pasture, dressed as an affluent traveler, approached Mansur, and pointed to a fat, prime lamb: 'Young shepherd, sell me that lamb for three gold dinars—which is thrice its market value! You can tell your master that a wolf snatched it in the rocky hills; no man will ever know!'

Mansur looked at the gold, and then at the stranger with calm, piercing eyes: 'You say that no man will know. But tell me, traveler: when my master asks where the lamb is, and I say "A wolf took it," where shall my conscience hide? The Creator sees the deed, my soul records the lie, and my honor will be forfeit for three pieces of gold. Take your money away; my master’s trust is not for sale.'

The sharper increased the offer to ten dinars, then twenty, and finally fifty gold dinars!

Mansur raised his shepherd’s crook and said sternly: 'If you offered me fifty thousand dinars, I would not betray the duty placed upon my shoulders! Begone before I summon my sheep-dogs!'

The sharper bowed his head in humble admiration. He returned to Cairo, paid his wager, and testified before all the merchants that in the pastures of Egypt lived a shepherd whose integrity was an unyielding rock against all the gold of the world.
moral: Unshakeable integrity and commitment to duty cannot be seduced by any wager.

quiz.question: What is the central moral lesson taught in "The Shepherd and the Rogue"?
options: Presence of mind and quiet wisdom triumph over brute strength.
Acting in haste and anger without thinking
Believing rumors and flattery without proof
